Shoot, I forgot all about "ingressclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class" (see plugin/pkg/admission/network/defaultingressclass/admission.go).  I edited my comment.

> I believe the problem could be simply solved if a controller was allowed by the ingress specification to optionally defines directly the class names it should look out for.

This is not part of the Ingress API, and nothing prevents ingress implementations from imposing their own restrictions or config.

The problem that remains is that *any* value you put into `IngressClassName` could, potentially, be a real class with an implementation looking for it.  That said, it's pretty unlikely that something like "namespace-private" or "namespace-$THISNS-private" would be used, and you can put anything there as long as you agree with yourself (the Ingress object and the implementation's flags).

> ingress-controller/ingress can works without read permission on cluster reosurce "IngressClass"

This sounds like a feature request. I think it's a big enough switch from the original design of Ingress that we should put forward a KEP.
We can come up with mechanisms that work namespaced, but we should aim for the formal review and buy-in that a KEP gets us.

>  they interpret the Ingress API specification to disallow their controller implementation to have such controller-specific config to identify ingresses based on .spec.ingressClassName.

Not an unreasonable interpretation, I guess.  That said, we don't usually enumerate all of the things that a non-conformant implementation is allowed to do. That's an open-ended list and would be noise for most readers of API docs.  

The way I interpret what we are talking about is "the controller can be configured to ignore the class".  That's it, right?  We are not talking about a conformance test, or saying that this is the right thing to do for cluster wide controller installations. This is about a very localized decision, perhaps a single namespace, to ignore some aspect of the spec.  There is some risk involved, as we discussed earlier, but it's plausible to make this "safe enough".

If there's a PR to be had here, it's just docs and needs to be somewhat insignificant. This is not the normal operating mode.  

If I misunderstood, and what you're really proposing is a deeper change to the specification to allow a namespaceed concept of class, then the other Tim is correct that it's a significant change and would require a kep.  That said, I don't think we're really entertaining significant changes to ingress API at this point. 

Also, if we make a docs change here, we should probably make a similar change to gateway API.

IMO: allowing a namespaced concept of class is only one of the potential fixes. We could define a label or annotation based mechanism for specifying something like an IngressClass, or we could look at an object reference mechanism, or… there are many options.

I think Kubernetes should clearly define that `ingressClassName` _is_ a reference to a name of a (cluster-scoped) IngressClass, which right now it is.

And we should also document that an ingress controller should be allowed to read IngressClasses, so that it can find the cluster default.

---

But if, for example, a particular ingress controller decides it's only interested in Ingresses that are labelled as:
- `foo.example/ingress-thingy: bananas`
- `foo.example/private-configuration-name: public-loadbalanced`

then that's basically fine. Nothing nonconformant has happened. Labels are there to let you do custom things (don't use official Kubernetes labels for this kind of detail).


We could define one well-known official label for Ingresses to indicate that they don't want the default IngressClass to apply to them even with `ingressClassName` unset. Setting that label won't stop another ingress controller trying, but we could do that, and I can see it being useful to try. Or we could extend the API, but I don't see the appetite for us to do that.


I also think we should ask in-project ingress controller authors to watch out for unhelpful precedents.

> the .spec,ingressControllerName MUST point to a valid IngressClass resource

This is really not a MUST. If you want to delete an IngressClass, we're not going to enforce that you delete all Ingresses that reference it. You might have some broken workloads, watch out for doing this in prod, test your changes etc. But it's _allowed_.

>> the .spec,ingressControllerName MUST point to a valid IngressClass resource
>
> This is really not a MUST. If you want to delete an IngressClass, we're not going to enforce...

Correct - in almost every place where one object refs another, we do not ENFORCE it, but instead seek to reconcile.

> I think Kubernetes should clearly define that ingressClassName is a reference to a name of a (cluster-scoped) IngressClass

It already says "ingressClassName is the name of an IngressClass cluster resource."

> And we should also document that an ingress controller should be allowed to read IngressClasses

I don't mind having documentation (an "Ingress controller implementors guide" seems useful) but it's not API comment-docs (e.g. in openapi).  

> so that it can find the cluster default.

The controllers don't do this, there's admission control which handles that.  But yes, a cluster-wide Ingress controller needs to be able to read IngressClass objects.  That seemed self-evident to me, but I guess that's not universally shared :)  

Because ingress is not implemented in-tree, we do not have a canned ClusterRole for it.  Should we?  That seems OK to me, but also could be seen as a security risk?

> We could define one well-known official label for Ingresses to indicate that they don't want the default IngressClass to apply to them even with ingressClassName unset

I guess, but ....is it really worhtwhile?  Just about everything with a "SomethingClass" follows a similar pattern - if you do not specify your class, you get `<this one>` as the default.  It feels a little cylcic to provide another way to say "I know you want to apply the default but I don't want the default", which will likely be met with another one expressing "I am the cluster admin, dammit, and you will get a default".  Remember, anything we change here we need to at least consider changing for Gateway and probably PVC and ...

IOW, electing a default class provides a sort of invariant for the cluster - do we want to violate that?  Is that better than recommending that people actually install a real IngressClass named "ns-private" or something?

> recommending that people actually install a real IngressClass named "ns-private" or something?

Actually, I like that idea. The trouble is: you need a friendly cluster admin, and if you had one of those you mightn't be asking for advice about how to get round them.

This could be a blog article. I think the official docs are basically already right, and blog articles are allowed to mark where the author's opinion isn't 100% aligned with Kubernetes as a project.

> Actually, I like that idea. The trouble is: you need a friendly cluster admin, and if you had one of those you mightn't be asking for advice about how to get round them.

That exactly is the problem that triggered the issue - if an ingress controller is installed as part of a (large) application to handle that application´s ingresses, the permissions to read a cluster-wide resource like IngressClass are difficult to get from a cluster admin, let alone that it is inconvenient for the admin having to manage an ingressClass just for that app.

Using .spec,ingressClassName as the single hint for a controller to select ingress resources feels intuitive.  A parallel controller-defined selection mechanism (e.g. some label) and leaving the ingressClassName empty for these namespace-managed ingresses would introduce the need for that "I don´t want the default" hint for the default cluster-wide controller to ignore the ingress.

The gap is rather on the side of how the controller can determine the ingressClassNames it shall handle.  If the spec allowed a namespaced ingress controller to be configured directly which ingressClassName to avoid the need to read all ingressClass resources and find its matches would solve that.  I realize that this would require to relax the above statement, though:
> I think Kubernetes should clearly define that ingressClassName is a reference to a name of a (cluster-scoped) IngressClass

> The gap is rather on the side of how the controller can determine the ingressClassNames it shall handle.

`your-controller --this-namespace-only --class-pattern=^private-NS.*`

Controller looks up its own namespace and looks for Ingresses that match that pattern.  This is entirely under the controller's purvey.

>  If the spec allowed a namespaced ingress controller to ... avoid the need to read all ingressClass resources

The spec doesn't need to allow it.  You can do anything you want, as long as the name you pick is a) valid and b) not being used by a real class.

An analogy, maybe not ideal but it might help: there is a building code for emergency exits. The exit must open outwards and for high occupancy buildings there must be a bar you can push to open the door even when it is locked. If there is a glass panel it must be fireproof and cannot be frosted.

You want to use one of these doors for your bathroom. You ask the building control people if the regulations would allow using a frosted non-fireproof panel. The building regulations people say that this wouldn't pass code for a building exit door, but they also don't mind what kind of door you use for the bathroom in your own apartment.

Kubernetes probably won't change the API definition or field semantics here, but if you're running your own cluster: you don't need to worry too much about what Kubernetes, as a project, thinks about your cluster.

If you buy the door and it reads EXIT, you can paint over it no problem. It's your door.

The difference to your analogy is that not many people will want an emergency exit door for their bathroom, whereas there is demand for namespaced ingress controllers.  That worked earlier and got broken with the switch to ingressClasses.  

This thread was not about what I could do in my own private cluster, it was rather about how an ingress  controller team that wants to be well-behaving in the Kubernetes ecosystem can keep the namespaced controller scenario alive.

To conclude the long thread, the options are

(1) go along the lines of @thockin's "_Controller looks up its own namespace and looks for Ingresses that match that pattern. This is entirely under the controller's purvey_" in the nginx-ingress-controller, with the caveat that the spec does not specifically support this, it just does not disallow it
(2) don't set the .spec.ingressClassName in the Ingress, and hope that there's no undesired side-effect from the default ingress controller picking up these ingresses.
(3) accept that the namespace-only concept got broken and ask the cluster admin to create an extra ingressClass per each namespaced app

Option 4: build an argument for extending the validation on this field to include values that can't possibly be real, and document them as reserved for private implementations, or something.  To make this argument we would have to bring the gateway API in alignment. I can't see why doing it for one and not the other would make sense
If we do it [make an API change] for IngressClass, does that set a precedent for StorageClass and other similar APIs? (and, if so, is that a problem)

Ingress and Gateway: YES
Storage: Maybe

> Option 4: build an argument for extending the validation on this field to include values that can't possibly be real, and document them as reserved for private implementations, or something.

this would be, for example, to mandate that such controller-configured class names could contain an invalid character (e.g. must start with an underscore) to ensure there's no collisions with real storageClass resources.   That would work.

> If we do it for IngressClass, does that set a precedent for StorageClass

There is currently no enforcement that PV and PVC references to StorageClasses are actually real StorageClass resources.  An admin can provision storage and create a PV for that storage with a .spec.storageClassName of the admin's choice, and a PVC will get bound if it requests a volume of that storageClassName.   I perceive that as intuitive; the admin acts like a storage provisioner and uses the regular storage class concept as an indication of the type of storage, and the PV-PVC binding works with the same matching rules.

> this would be, for example, to mandate that such controller-configured class names could contain an invalid character (e.g. must start with an underscore) to ensure there's no collisions with real storageClass resources. That would work.

That change needs a KEP, which means it needs contributor effort to make it happen. We can do it, but there are other priorities for the project that may come first.

I will also say that the bar for changes to Ingress is really high - it's essentially a frozen API.  Not impossible but the change needs to be VERY surgical and VERY thoroughly considered for side-effect.
@thockin @sftim if that is the case, can we say option 01 is more practical. not sure if we should suggest ingress-controller vendor to resolve this issue with option-01?

title: DRA: Extra unexpected devices allocated when using 'allocationMode: All'
body:
### What happened?

I was testing the ability to allocate both node-local resources (GPUs) along with a new network attached resource called an IMEX channel.

My setup is as follows:
* 8 nodes with 1 GPU each
* 2 pools of IMEX channels (with 10 available in each)
* IMEX channels from the first pool are part of "IMEX domain 1" and can be attached to nodes 0-3
* IMEX channels from the second pool are part of "IMEX domain 2" and can be attached to nodes 4-7

With this setup, I create two ResourceClaims, one ResourceClaim template, and 2 deployments. The two resource Claims are for two distinct IMEX channels, the ResourceClaimTemplate is for all GPUs on a given node, and the 2 deployments (of 4 replicas each) consume these claims / claimtemplates across each replica in order to simulate running 2 MPI jobs across two different IMEX domains.

Here are the specs:
```
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: imex-test1
---
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1alpha3
kind: ResourceClaim
metadata:
  namespace: imex-test1
  name: shared-imex-channel0
spec:
  devices:
    requests:
    - name: channel
      deviceClassName: imex.nvidia.com
---
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1alpha3
kind: ResourceClaim
metadata:
  namespace: imex-test1
  name: shared-imex-channel1
spec:
  devices:
    requests:
    - name: channel
      deviceClassName: imex.nvidia.com
---
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1alpha3
kind: ResourceClaimTemplate
metadata:
  namespace: imex-test1
  name: all-node-gpus
spec:
  spec:
    devices:
      requests:
      - name: all-gpus
        deviceClassName: gpu.nvidia.com
        allocationMode: All
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  namespace: imex-test1
  name: pod0
  labels:
    app: imex-test1-pod0
spec:
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: pod0
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: pod0
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: ctr
        image: ubuntu:22.04
        command: ["bash", "-c"]
        args: ["trap 'exit 0' TERM; sleep 9999 & wait"]
        resources:
          claims:
          - name: gpus
          - name: imex-channel
      resourceClaims:
      - name: gpus
        resourceClaimTemplateName: all-node-gpus
      - name: imex-channel
        resourceClaimName: shared-imex-channel0
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  namespace: imex-test1
  name: pod1
  labels:
    app: imex-test1-pod1
spec:
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: pod1

        app: pod1
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: ctr

        command: ["bash", "-c"]
        args: ["trap 'exit 0' TERM; sleep 9999 & wait"]

          - name: imex-channel
      resourceClaims:
      - name: gpus
        resourceClaimTemplateName: all-node-gpus
      - name: imex-channel
        resourceClaimName: shared-imex-channel1
```

When I run this, I do not get the resource allocated to each pod in each deployment as expected (instead all pods remain pending forever).

However, If I change to explicitly requesting 1 GPU from a node instead of using `allocationMode: All`, things work as expected.

One thing to note is that the code linked below doesn't consider the CEL expression selector in the `gpu.nvidia.com` and `imex.nvidia.com` device classes when calculating `requestData.numDevices`. That might be factor in this somehow:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/52095a8b7b9b75d67a3882a21a6647e4f90ade48/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/allocator.go#L176-L210

### What did you expect to happen?

My expectation was that we would see 4 pods from each deployment with the following set of resources:

**deployment 0, pod0**:
1 GPU from a node in the same IMEX domain as all other pods in deployment 0
IMEX channel 0 from the same IMEX domain as all other pods in deployment 0

**deployment 0, pod1**:
1 GPU from a node in the same IMEX domain as all other pods in deployment 0
IMEX channel 0 from the same IMEX domain as all other pods in deployment 0

IMEX channel 0 from the same IMEX domain as all other pods in deployment 0

**deployment 1, pod0**:
1 GPU from a node in the same IMEX domain as all other pods in deployment 1
IMEX channel 0 from the same IMEX domain as all other pods in deployment 1

**deployment 1, pod1**:
1 GPU from a node in the same IMEX domain as all other pods in deployment 1
IMEX channel 0 from the same IMEX domain as all other pods in deployment 1

**deployment 1, pod2**:
1 GPU from a node in the same IMEX domain as all other pods in deployment 1

**deployment 1, pod3**:

root@k8s-master01:~/finalizer-operator-master# kubectl logs pod -f
2024/09/22 04:00:08 应用程序启动
2024/09/22 04:00:08 应用程序正在运行...
2024/09/22 04:01:07 收到信号: terminated, 正在关闭应用程序...

root@k8s-master01:~/trident-operator# kubectl exec -it pod -- tail -f /tmp/my-termination-message


command terminated with exit code 137


```
package main

import (
    "log"
    "os"
    "os/signal"
    "syscall"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    // 设置日志
    logFile, err := os.OpenFile("app.log", os.O_CREATE|os.O_WRONLY|os.O_APPEND, 0666)
    
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatalf("error opening log file: %v", err)
    }
    defer logFile.Close()

    log.SetOutput(os.Stdout)
    log.Println("应用程序启动")

    // 创建一个 channel 用于接收系统信号
    sigs := make(chan os.Signal, 1)
    // 监听 SIGTERM 和 SIGINT 信号
    signal.Notify(sigs, syscall.SIGTERM, syscall.SIGINT)

    go func() {
        // 等待接收信号
        sig := <-sigs
        log.Printf("收到信号: %s, 正在关闭应用程序...", sig)
        // 模拟清理工作
        time.Sleep(2 * time.Second)
        log.Println("清理工作完成，应用程序已关闭")
        time.Sleep(20 * time.Second)
```

title: scheduler: Pods aren't retried at all with cluster events to unschedulable Pod
body:
It's initially raised at https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/110175#issuecomment-1140397251. Just create a separate issue so that we don't forget.

So, currently, we don't trigger requeueing with cluster events to unschedulable Pods. It's OK for in-tree plugins, but not OK for out-of-tree plugins that could change the scheduling results with unsched Pods state.

/sig scheduling
/kind bug
/cc @macsko

title: Garbage collector never starts when it fails initial cache sync
body:
### What happened?

When running a kind cluster in HA mode, if KCM's garbage collector fails its initial sync, it never starts. As a result, completed job pods are never cleaned up after the `ttlSecondsAfterFinished ` is reached.

### What did you expect to happen?

I'd expect that one resource failing to sync would not block the garbage collection of other resources.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Kind cluster in [HA mode](https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/docs/user/quick-start/#control-plane-ha).
2. Create the CRD, a custom resource with two versions and webhook strategy set to conversion ([crd.yaml](https://gist.github.com/rschalo/5a290a87a7c995cdfdd44e1165a2eac2#file-crd-yaml) and [cr.yaml](https://gist.github.com/rschalo/5a290a87a7c995cdfdd44e1165a2eac2#file-cr-yaml))

```
E0904 01:50:06.546595       1 shared_informer.go:316] unable to sync caches for garbage collector
```

title: [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Change in version-skewed behavior in v1.31
body:
For features that span nodes & control planes, they must support the case where the feature is enabled in the control plane but not on nodes, in order to support version skew after the feature is promoted to a default-on state.

Previously, the node/control-plane skewed behavior of `InPlacePodVerticalScaling` was to sort of support the resize by restarting the resized container. The API is eventually consistent with the running container.

1. Someone / something updates pod resources on a running pod
2. apiserver has the feature gate enabled, so it accepts the request and sets the resize status to pending
3. Kubelet sees a change in the hash and restarts the container, with the new resource amount
4. Kubelet patches the status, but doesn't set the resize status (and doesn't copy it from the old status), thus clearing it

In v1.31 the hashing logic was changed to avoid accidental container restarts: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/124220. However, this also prevents the Kubelet from seeing the changed resources in step 3, so the container is not restarted with the new resource value. If the container is restarted for any other reason, it will be restarted with the new resource value. There is no way to tell from the API which value the container is using.

The previous behavior is consistent with the skew handling described in the KEP, except this part was never implemented:
> kubelet: When feature-gate is disabled, if kubelet sees a Proposed resize, it rejects the resize as Infeasible.

This is a regression, but shouldn't be release blocking as it is only triggered when the alpha feature is enabled.

/kind bug
/kind regression
/milestone v1.31
/sig node
/priority important-longterm

nodes.body:
**Proposal:**

The `Resources` field in container status is set by the Kubelet if and only if IPPVS is enabled. It's a hack, but the apiserver can use this information to determine whether the node the pod is running on supports IPPVS. In other words, in validation, only allow a resize if the resources field is present on the container status (or if the pod is still pending):

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/apis/core/validation/validation.go#L5166

If we make this change in v1.32 (beta), I think we can safely ignore the change in version skew behavior.

> In v1.31 the hashing logic was changed to avoid accidental container restarts: #124220. However, this also prevents the Kubelet from seeing the changed resources in step 3, so the container is not restarted with the new resource value. If the container is restarted for any other reason, it will be restarted with the new resource value.

I believe the current behavior is reasonable. We shouldn't restart the pod just because a user updates pod resources when the InPlacePodVerticalScaling feature gate is enabled on the ApiServer (this is still unexpected for users).



> in validation, only allow a resize if the resources field is present on the container status (or if the pod is still pending):

Should we modify the ApiServer's validation logic based on Kubelet's behavior? Would it be better to warn users that this behavior will cause the actual running pod's resources to be inconsistent with their updates until the pod is restarted?

> kubelet: When feature-gate is disabled, if kubelet sees a Proposed resize, it rejects the resize as Infeasible.

~I believe the current actions are still in line with this goal, aren't they?~
/assign

>> in validation, only allow a resize if the resources field is present on the container status (or if the pod is still pending):
>
> Should we modify the ApiServer's validation logic based on Kubelet's behavior? Would it be better to warn users that this behavior will cause the actual running pod's resources to be inconsistent with their updates until the pod is restarted?

I agree it's weird, but I think it's our best option here. We can remove it in a future release once we're not worried about the version skew.

I wanted to capture this issue so we don't forget about it, but I think the next step is to update the KEP (I'm working on a KEP update).

/cc @thockin

>> kubelet: When feature-gate is disabled, if kubelet sees a Proposed resize, it rejects the resize as Infeasible.
>
> I believe the current actions are still in line with this goal, aren't they?

I'm not sure I understand what you're saying here. The Kubelet doesn't currently reject a proposed resize if the feature gate is disabled. If we wanted this to be the version skew behavior, we'd need to push that change in v1.32, and then wait all the way until v1.35 to promote to beta.

> I'm not sure I understand what you're saying here. The Kubelet doesn't currently reject a proposed resize if the feature gate is disabled. If we wanted this to be the version skew behavior, we'd need to push that change in v1.32, and then wait all the way until v1.35 to promote to beta.

Soory,  my previous response wasn't accurate.


> I agree it's weird, but I think it's our best option here. We can remove it in a future release once we're not worried about the version skew.

If it was our consensus in previous discussions(in KEP's PR) that we should reject resource updates to running pods when the `InPlacePodVerticalScaling` feature gate is enabled on the ApiServer but not on the kubelet, then I support that approach.

If we consider the issue as "no way to tell from the API which value the container is using," the original KEP seems to have the same problem.

When the ApiServer receives the user's update to the pod resource, and the kubelet rejects the resizing, the resources in the running pod remain old, while the pod resources in the ApiServer are updated. From this perspective, the current behavior seems consistent with the original KEP.

The only difference is that the kubelet does not explicitly reject the resource update.
Hey Folks, why is this in the 1.31 milestone? (We are shipping 1.31.0 tomorrow)

agreed, I don't think this is actionable for the 1.31 milestone

/milestone clear

Yeah, sorry, I originally tagged v1.31 because the change in behavior is in v1.31, and I thought we might want to try and backport a fix, but I don't think that will be needed (and certainly isn't needed for v1.31.0)

> Should we modify the ApiServer's validation logic based on Kubelet's behavior?

Any feature which has updates control-plane and node components has this issue, more or less - right?

I don't think we want to gate the APi based on kubelets - Is it "some" kubelets?  All kubelets?  What if one is updated and rolled back after API admission.

> Any feature which has updates control-plane and node components has this issue, more or less - right?
> 
> I don't think we want to gate the APi based on kubelets - Is it "some" kubelets? All kubelets? What if one is updated and rolled back after API admission.

Yes, this approach (gating the API based on the kubelet) cannot cover scenarios where the kubelet is rolled back. This proposal by @tallclair is more of a remedial action because our current behavior has disrupted the version skew policy outlined in the original KEP(even though we haven't actually implemented this).

However, I would prefer to discuss the rationality of the version skew policy in the original KEP. If we require the kubelet to explicitly reject updates to pod resources when the InPlacePodVerticalScaling feature gate is not enabled, then to ensure our component version skew policy is maintained, the feature gate would need at least three versions to reach beta(even though we've already gone through four versions in the alpha stage).

I believe a more common version skew policy would be to have the kubelet ignore the pod resource updates when the feature gate is not enabled (like we added a new field to podSpec, but the old version of kubelet will ignore it). This approach does not impact running workloads. The downside, however, is that the actual running resources of a pod may not match what is observed through the API until the pod is restarted (The version skew policy in the original KEP seems to have the same problem).

Regarding the InPlacePodVerticalScaling feature gate, if the Apiserver is enabled but the kubelet has it disabled, the behavior is as follows:

Original KEP: If the kubelet detects a Proposed resize, it rejects the resize as Infeasible.

Before #124220: If the kubelet detects a Proposed resize, it would restart the pod with the updated resources and clear the resize field in the status.

After #124220: If the kubelet detects a Proposed resize, it does not restart the pod and clear the resize field in the status.

I prefer the current approach, WDYT？

Of course, no matter what we choose, we need to modify the KEP, because we have deviated from it.
/triage accepted

>> Should we modify the ApiServer's validation logic based on Kubelet's behavior?
> 
> Any feature which has updates control-plane and node components has this issue, more or less - right?

Yes, more or less. We should probably solve this in a generic way, but I'd prefer not to block in-place pod resize on it. This is also an unusual case since it's not adding a new field (or value), just making an existing one mutable.

> I don't think we want to gate the APi based on kubelets - Is it "some" kubelets? All kubelets? What if one is updated and rolled back after API admission.

I'll propose a KEP update with the details, but here's a rough summary:

- This logic is only applied on update, and the gating only happens if the pod is already bound to a node (there's some details to work out around whether the pod is pending)
- The gating I proposed above is based on whether the Kubelet is setting a specific status field, so if there are mixed node versions, it would be blocked for nodes with the feature disabled, but allowed for enabled nodes
- Rollback isn't an issue, since this is only evaluated on update by comparing to the old value. Once the value is updated, this validation logic doesn't kick in, independent of whether the feature is enabled or disabled.

> After https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/124220: If the kubelet detects a Proposed resize, it does not restart the pod and clear the resize field in the status.
> 
> I prefer the current approach, WDYT？

I don't like that there is no way to tell what resources the container is configured for in the current approach, and when it uses the updated resources is non-deterministic. I could also imagine this causing problems with any controllers that try to use in-place update (e.g. VPA).

If we go with either of the current approaches, IMO we should backport a change to make the behavior consistent.

> I don't like that there is no way to tell what resources the container is configured for in the current approach, and when it uses the updated resources is non-deterministic.

I thought the status was supposed to give visibility for when the node had accepted the increased resources. Does it not?

> If we go with either of the current approaches, IMO we should backport a change to make the behavior consistent.

I don't think we'd backport changes for alpha features, we'd wait until the oldest supported skewed node had the behavior we expected before enabling by default, right?

>> I don't like that there is no way to tell what resources the container is configured for in the current approach, and when it uses the updated resources is non-deterministic.
> 
> I thought the status was supposed to give visibility for when the node had accepted the increased resources. Does it not?

Only once the feature is enabled. The discussion here is specifically for the skewed case where it's enabled in the apiserver, so the resources can be mutated, but the Kubelet doesn't have in-place updates enabled. As of v1.31 the behavior is that the resources are updated, but the Kubelet ignores them until the container is restarted for any other reason.

> I don't think we'd backport changes for alpha features, we'd wait until the oldest supported skewed node had the behavior we expected before enabling by default, right?

Yeah, probably. Hence wanting to address it at the control plane :)
@thockin @SergeyKanzhelev  Do you have any additional thoughts on this? If not, I will go ahead and implement it according to @tallclair's suggestion.

This is fixed with the new version skew handling described in the [KEP](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-node/1287-in-place-update-pod-resources/README.md#version-skew-strategy). https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/117767 tracks the version skew strategy implementation, so I'll close this.

@HirazawaUi feel free to pick up https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/117767

title: Scheduler allows more volumes than a CSI driver limit to be attached
body:
### What happened?

When a pod that uses an attachable volume is deleted, it can take some time for its volumes to get detached, but the scheduler does not care about it and treats Pod volumes as detached immediately after Pod is deleted from the API server.

The scheduler should count not only Pods, but also existing VolumeAttachment objects to get accurate nr. of volumes attached to the node.


### What did you expect to happen?

Scheduler respects the attachment limit and never puts more Pods with volumes when a CSI driver is still detaching a volume for a deleted pod.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Get a CSI driver that reports an attach limit. Using AWS EBS, it reports 26 max. attachments in its CSINode:
    ```yaml
    spec:
      drivers:
      - allocatable:
          count: 26
        name: ebs.csi.aws.com
    ```
2. Create many pods targeting the same node using a `nodeSelector`, each of them using its own AWS EBS PV.
3. See scheduler tries to schedule just 26 Pods on the node, the rest is Pending.
4. Delete one Running Pod. Once the Pod is deleted, the scheduler puts a new Pod to the node immediately. But the volume of the deleted Pod is still attached!
5. Observe that nr. of VolumeAttachments is >26 for a short time. Depending on the driver and its current load and nr. of deleted pods it may not be that short time and it may grow significantly over 26.

Most CSI drivers recover from this, however, e.g. AWS EBS driver throws really weird errors and the recovery takes some time and I don't blame the driver.

### Anything else we need to know?

All attachable in-tree volumes are now migrated to CSI and have VolumeAttachments, so the calculation will be accurate even for them.

title: EventedPLEG: Timestamp in PodStatus for Generic PLEG should be more accurate
body:
### What happened?

When the `EventedPLEG` feature is enabled, GenericPLEG also works for backing up the EventedPLEG. In case both PLEGs update the same pod status in the cache at the almost same time, `Timestamp` was introduced to `PodSandboxStatusResponse` in the CRI API ([KEP](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/3386-kubelet-evented-pleg#timestamp-of-the-pod-status)). This timestamp (`PodSandboxStatusResponse.Timestamp`) is recorded in seconds while the timestamp in an event (`ContainerEventResponse.CreatedAt`) is recorded in nanoseconds. So, these timestamps cannot be compared accurately.

- Evented PLEG uses a timestamp in `ContainerEventResponse.CreatedAt` for the cache. This is set in nanoseconds in runtimes ([CRI-O code](https://github.com/cri-o/cri-o/blob/74d54cd3071c51225055df91121ebf77618e86a8/server/server.go#L934)) (though there is a bug (#124297) that kubelet treats it as seconds).
- Generic PLEG uses a timestamp in `PodSandboxStatusResponse.Timestamp` for the cache:
  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a2106b5f73fe9352f7bc0520788855d57fc301e1/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L1583
  This value is set in seconds by [CRI-O](https://github.com/cri-o/cri-o/blob/74d54cd3071c51225055df91121ebf77618e86a8/server/sandbox_status.go#L43-L65) while [containerd](https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/2ddd3db9524b14000208862e2e578e567b391a06/internal/cri/server/sandbox_status.go#L85-L88) does not look to set it (though there is another issue (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/125624#issuecomment-2254396844) regarding containerd case). 


### What did you expect to happen?

`PodSandboxStatusResponse.Timestamp` should be recorded in nanoseconds.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

It is difficult to reproduce this race intentionally on Kubernetes.

The following sample code simulates the problem:
```
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"time"
)

func main() {
	eventedTime := time.Now().UnixNano()
	time.Sleep(100 * time.Millisecond)
	genericTime := time.Now().Unix()

	cachedEventedTime := time.Unix(0, eventedTime)
	cachedGenericTime := time.Unix(genericTime, 0)

	if cachedEventedTime.Before(cachedGenericTime) {
		fmt.Printf("Expected: evented:%v, generic:%v\n", cachedEventedTime, cachedGenericTime)
	} else {
		fmt.Printf("Unexpected: evented:%v, generic:%v\n", cachedEventedTime, cachedGenericTime)
	}
}
```

```
$ go run timestamp.go 
Unexpected: evented:2024-07-28 13:57:26.329366032 +0200 CEST, generic:2024-07-28 13:57:26 +0200 CEST
```


### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

Current master (1.31)


### Cloud provider

N/A

### OS version

<details>

```console
# On Linux:
$ cat /etc/os-release
# paste output here
$ uname -a
# paste output here

# On Windows:
C:\> wmic os get Caption, Version, BuildNumber, OSArchitecture
# paste output here
```

</details>


### Install tools

<details>

</details>


### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable)

This issue could happen with CRI-O, which sets `Timestamp` to `PodSandboxStatusResponse`.


### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)

<details>

cc @harche @sairameshv
/triage accepted
/priority important-longterm
As mentioned in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/124297#issuecomment-2341375744, this has been fixed in CRI-O (cri-o/cri-o/pull/8582).

I wonder if we may need to handle a case where CRI-O without the fix is used. Like treating seconds (too small value for nanoseconds) as zero:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/e35bd86edd66a956e4de409f207bced2c66efb7a/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L1567-L1568

Now that CRI-O fixed the timestamp for v1.32, we need to fix it in kubernetes for v1.32. Otherwise, I guess EventedPLEG would not work with CRI-O.

Without fixing it in Kubernetes, Generic PLEG would set a too large timestamp to the cache. This would prevent EventedPLEG from updating the cache. As a result, container statuses would be updated only by Generic PLEG which relists pods every five minutes.

The fix in CRI-O has been also backpoted to older versions.  Because #124297 is not backported to Kubernetes 1.31 and older, both Evented PLEG and Generic PLEG will convert timestamps in nanoseconds to seconds. These timestamps can be compared. I don’t think a critical problem will occur in older versions.

title: [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Infeasible resize is actuated by restarting container
body:
### What happened?

If a container is restarted along with an exit while its resizing is stuck in `Infeasible` or `Deferred`, the unacceptable resizing is actuated:
1. Request an infeasible resize (exceeds node allocatable cpu):
    ```
   $ kubectl patch pod resize-pod --patch '{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"resize-container", "resources":{"requests":{"cpu":"100"}, "limits":{"cpu":"100"}}}]}}'
   pod/resize-pod patched

    ```
2. Kill the container manually (`restartPolicy` is `Always`):
   ```
   $ kubectl exec resize-pod -- kill 1
   ```
3. Then, it looks still stuck in `Infeasible` or `Deferred` on the API pod status. However, the cgroup of the container is configured as requested:
   ```
   $ kubectl get pod resize-pod -o jsonpath='{.status.resize}'
   Infeasible
   ```
   ```
   $ kubectl exec resize-pod -- cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max
   10000000 100000
   # 10000000 = newLimit(100) * 1000mCPU * period(100000) / 1000mCPU
   ```
   ```
   $ kubectl exec resize-pod -- cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.weight
   3906
   # 3906 = ((newRequest(100) * 1000mCPU * SharesPerCPU(1024) / 1000mCPU) - 2 ) * 9999 / 262142
   ```

However, it does not seem that this issue affects actual resource consumption. Because the pod cgroup is not updated in this case, the container resource will keep limited. In addition, since `AllocatedResources` in the container is not updated, this infeasible resizing will not affect the pod resource calculation of the scheduler.

### What did you expect to happen?

This killed container is restarted with the old spec.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Enable `InPlacePodVerticalScaling`.
2. Create a pod whose restartPolicy is `Always`:
    <details>

   ```
   apiVersion: v1
   kind: Pod
   metadata:
     creationTimestamp: null
     labels:
       run: resize-pod
     name: resize-pod
   spec:
     containers:
     - image: busybox
       name: resize-container
       command:
         - sh
         - -c
         - trap "exit 0" SIGTERM; while true; do sleep 1; done
       resources:
         requests:
           cpu: 200m
           memory: 200Mi
         limits:
           cpu: 200m
           memory: 200Mi
       resizePolicy:
       - resourceName: cpu
         restartPolicy: NotRequired
       - resourceName: memory
         restartPolicy: NotRequired
     restartPolicy: Always
   ```

    </details>
3. Request an infeasible resize:
   ```
   kubectl patch pod resize-pod --patch '{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"resize-container", "resources":{"requests":{"cpu":"100"}, "limits":{"cpu":"100"}}}]}}'
   ```
4. Kill the container:
   ```
   kubectl exec resize-pod -- kill 1
   ```

   

### Anything else we need to know?

By executing `kubectl get --watch`, we can see the resized status in a moment:
```
$ kubectl get pod resize-pod -o jsonpath='spec: {.spec.containers[0].resources}{"\nallocatedResources: "}{.status.containerStatuses[0].allocatedResources}{"\nstatus: "}{.status.containerStatuses[0].resources}{"\nresize: "}{.status.resize}{"\n"}' -w
spec: {"limits":{"cpu":"100","memory":"200Mi"},"requests":{"cpu":"100","memory":"200Mi"}}
allocatedResources: {"cpu":"200m","memory":"200Mi"}
status: {"limits":{"cpu":"100","memory":"200Mi"},"requests":{"cpu":"100","memory":"200Mi"}}  # <- See this line
resize: 
spec: {"limits":{"cpu":"100","memory":"200Mi"},"requests":{"cpu":"100","memory":"200Mi"}}
allocatedResources: {"cpu":"200m","memory":"200Mi"}
status: {"limits":{"cpu":"200m","memory":"200Mi"},"requests":{"cpu":"200m","memory":"200Mi"}}
resize: Infeasible
```

The resized pod status is set here:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/37f733a657ef71d66177d00f9b7d47ec507dedd3/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L1802
However, the pod status is overwritten with an old pod status immediately here:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/37f733a657ef71d66177d00f9b7d47ec507dedd3/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2820

This issue is mentioned in another issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/125205#issuecomment-2143532151

```console
$ kubectl version
```

title: client-go: global transport cache grows unbounded when requesting configs with non-nil `Dial` functions
body:
### What happened?

client-go 1.26+ changed the semantics of `kubernetes.NewForConfig(restConfig)` by caching TLS transport objects in some cases which were not cached in earlier versions (notably, configurations with non-nil `Dial` functions).

Unfortunately the cache does not have any expire or pruning mechanism, leading in worst case to unbounded growth of memory usage (see for example kubernetes/kubernetes#117250).

The change is: kubernetes/kubernetes#112450

This issue is for a program using client-go (Rancher) requesting clientsets with non-nil Dial functions over time.

### What did you expect to happen?

TLS transport objects not to be internally cached by client-go, like in 1.25 and earlier versions.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

`	clientset, err := kubernetes.NewForConfig(config)`

with `config.Dial` being non-nil.

I will be submitting a PR that unit-test covers this.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

1.26 and over

/assign

Thanks Ben :)
/triage accepted

I think the question is: Do we want to support a blunt "no more caching" knob for users (@moio has a PR proposed for this in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/125819) which does pretty conclusively handle that use case, or do we want to try to further mitigate the issue by default instead? (which may also solve some other issue that are cropping up, without adding another config field)

cc ~@liggit~ @aojea @enj @dims
cc @liggitt ... dropped a t there ...
@BenTheElder i am not opposed to what @moio has in there. I would love to have a fix for everyone more.

> with `config.Dial` being non-nil.

with config.Dial non-nil you have to use something like https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/117258, is that not solving the problem?

No, it is not solving the problem.

My understanding is:

 - client-go < 1.26 did **not** cache TLS transport objects if `config.Dial` is non-nil, but such caching is necessary in Kubernetes, so it was implemented inside `AvailableConditionController`.

 - client-go >= 1.26 changed that, and TLS transport objects **are** now cached by client-go. Therefore https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/117258 was merged in order to avoid caching in both places, and in fact it drops the cache in `AvailableConditionController`:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/117258/files#diff-f768db209f4057d77a95bb4dc5cf166b8dde189398590809600f96417735e9edL169


In my case (Rancher), I have the "dual" problem: I do not want any caching to happen, because the `config.Dial` functions are many and change frequently.

 - client-go < 1.26 did **not** cache TLS transport and my code was fine
 - client-go >= 1.26 **does**, and I see no way to prevent that

Hence this PR to add an optional, disabled-by-default flag to restore the previous behavior if necessary (and give users a way to implement a different caching mechanism if they so want).

Does that make sense?

do you have some links to the specific code you are referring so I can get some context?

Are you mutating the same config with different dialers every time?

> do you have some links to the specific code you are referring so I can get some context?

Yes, but that is a bit buried, I hope I'll do a decent job explaining the situation.

First of all Rancher is an application to manage multiple Kubernetes clusters, therefore it keeps track of clusters "registered" to it.

There is a [ToRESTConfig](https://github.com/rancher/rancher/blob/3c1c5730afc57546b362b2010744efdc7b77212b/pkg/clustermanager/manager.go#L259-L342) function to generate a `rest.Config` given Rancher-specific `v3.Cluster` object, which represents a registered cluster. The resulting `rest.Config` is of course used to manage the cluster.

Among other things, `ToRESTConfig` calls a [ClusterDialer](https://github.com/rancher/rancher/blob/3c1c5730afc57546b362b2010744efdc7b77212b/pkg/clustermanager/manager.go#L291) method, which returns a dialing function for the specific `Cluster`.

That dialing function is crucial for Rancher, because different clusters are accessed in different ways depending on network topology and other factors. Importantly, most clusters are accessed via a Rancher-specific tunneling mechanism called [remotedialer](https://github.com/rancher/remotedialer): `ClusterDialer` takes care of that, and therefore we almost universally have a `Dialer` in our `rest.Config`.

> Are you mutating the same config with different dialers every time?

No, we are generating new configs every time. Because managed clusters can be many, they are divided among Rancher replicas to implement load balancing. When "rebalancing" events happen, replicas get to connect to a different set of clusters than before.

After rebalancing a replica they might get new clusters, in that case `rest.Config`s are simply generated from scratch.

Or it could lose some, and in that case any stale `rest.Config`s are discarded. But the TLS Transport remains cached inside of client-go, therefore causing a leak.

I hope this helps
@aojea are there any news about this one?

@aojea thanks for the deep dive, I think I now understand your line of reasoning. 

I will admit I am not particularly happy about copying over that much code from [transport/cache.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7436ca32bc766ff202109a7541d2e7bb41ee7d13/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/transport/cache.go#L96-L137) as it may diverge in future client-go versions, although it's probably a viable workaround.

My final question now is: do you consider https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/125819 not acceptable because such workaround is possible?

Thanks

> My final question now is: do you consider #125819 not acceptable because such workaround is possible?

not because of the workaroun @liggitt has more historical context about client-go than me, IMHO this package already exposes a lot of internal details and it also has dependencies with another things that make it hard to support.

Ideally I think people should build their own transports and httpclient and use `RESTClientForConfigAndClient`

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/95b3fe9f15cdcaf98098be398478e70365b12dd7/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/rest/config.go#L332-L338
[seems we lack consensus to go forward with this, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/125818#issuecomment-2315167931 sounds pretty reasonable to me]

title: [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] resources in pod status are never updated if EventedPLEG is enabled
body:
### What happened?

If eventedPLEG is enabled, resources in a pod status are never updated after the pod is resized.


### What did you expect to happen?

Resources in a pod status are updated after the pod is resized.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Enable `EventedPLEG` and `InPlacePodVerticalScaling`.
2. Create a pod and update resources in the pod following the [documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/resize-container-resources/#updating-the-pod-s-resources).

```
$ kubectl -n qos-example patch pod qos-demo-5 --patch '{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"qos-demo-ctr-5", "resources":{"requests":{"cpu":"800m"}, "limits":{"cpu":"800m"}}}]}}'
$ # Wait for more than 10 minutes...
$ kubectl -n qos-example get pod qos-demo-5 -o json | jq '.status.containerStatuses[0].resources'
{
  "limits": {
    "cpu": "700m",
    "memory": "200Mi"
  },
  "requests": {
    "cpu": "700m",
    "memory": "200Mi"
  }
}
```


### Anything else we need to know?

The root cause of this issue is the same problem mentioned in #124297. Evented PLEG passes a timestamp wrongly to a cache:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5ec31e84d6c525c173906b1497ee6f075c1926e9/pkg/kubelet/pleg/evented.go#L269

EventedPLEG does not emit any event or update a cache because a runtime raises no event at resizing a container without restart. Though GenericPLEG is expected to back up in such a case, this does not work. Generic PLEG relists pods every 5 minutes. It also updates the cache when pod resizing is in progress:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5ec31e84d6c525c173906b1497ee6f075c1926e9/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2008-L2011

However, an update from GenericPLEG is rejected because the new timestamp looks older than the existing timestamp that EventedPLEG sets at starting the pod because of the bug mentioned above:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5ec31e84d6c525c173906b1497ee6f075c1926e9/pkg/kubelet/container/cache.go#L106-L112


### Kubernetes version

```console
$ kubectl version
# paste output here
```

Only fixing #124297 will not solve this issue. If the CRI runtime doesn't set a timestamp to `PodSandboxStatusResponse` for `PodSandboxStatus()`, the generic PLEG uses `0` as a timestamp to update the cache.

As of today, containerd does not look to set the timestamp while CRI-O does:
- containerd: https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/2ddd3db9524b14000208862e2e578e567b391a06/internal/cri/server/sandbox_status.go#L85-L88
- CRI-O: https://github.com/cri-o/cri-o/blob/74d54cd3071c51225055df91121ebf77618e86a8/server/sandbox_status.go#L52-L65

If the timestamp is not set by the runtime, the runtime manager in kubelet does not set the timestamp in `PodStatus`:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a2106b5f73fe9352f7bc0520788855d57fc301e1/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L1565-L1612

The generic PLEG uses `0` in the `PodStatus` to update the cache:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a2106b5f73fe9352f7bc0520788855d57fc301e1/pkg/kubelet/pleg/generic.go#L478-L482

We also need to fix this problem.
/assign

~I noticed this issue will not been solved even if the timestamp issues are fixed. Generic PLEG updates a pod status only when container statuses in the pod changed. A pod is resized while containers are running.~

~Only when a pod is resized soon after it was created, Generic PLEG can update resource information because Generic PLEG relists pods every five minutes. This happens only in testing.~
~Alternatively, #125635 may fix this issue as a side-effect.~

> I noticed this issue will not been solved even if the timestamp issues are fixed. Generic PLEG updates a pod status only when container statuses in the pod changed. A pod is resized while containers are running.
> 
> Only when a pod is resized soon after it was created, Generic PLEG can update resource information because Generic PLEG relists pods every five minutes. This happens only in testing.

I misunderstood. Generic PLEG updates the cache here when a pod is being resized:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ee74baec6e05afde972f1a8705d4f8efe066f120/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L1980
So, this issue will be solved by the timestamp fix.

Because of #127195, a timestamp is set to `PodStatus` even if containerd does not set the timestamp. So, this issue has been fixed.

note: containerd will set the timestamp in the future release due to containerd/containerd#10740.

title: Named ports in initContainer sidecars do not work with NetworkPolicies
body:
### What happened?

We have recently migrated our traditional sidecar definitions to the new recommended initContainer sidecars.

We are running a CockroachDB StatefulSet that has a Vault sidecar, such that members 0 and 1 have a "legacy" sidecar container:

```console
$ kubectl --context prod-aws -n partner-registration get -o json pod cockroachdb-0 | jq -r '.spec.containers[] | select(.name == "vault-credentials-agent") | .ports'
[
  {
    "containerPort": 8099,
    "name": "metrics",
    "protocol": "TCP"
  }
]

$ kubectl --context prod-aws -n partner-registration get -o json pod cockroachdb-1 | jq -r '.spec.containers[] | select(.name == "vault-credentials-agent") | .ports'
[
  {
    "containerPort": 8099,
    "name": "metrics",
    "protocol": "TCP"
  }
]
```

And member 2 has a new initContainer style sidecar:

```console
$ kubectl --context prod-aws -n partner-registration get -o json pod cockroachdb-2 | jq -r '.spec.initContainers[] | select(.name == "vault-credentials-agent") | .ports[]'
{
  "containerPort": 8099,
  "name": "metrics",
  "protocol": "TCP"
}
```

They all expose a named port `metrics`.

We also have a NetworkPolicy in this namespace such that:

```console
$ kubectl --context prod-aws -n partner-registration get netpol private-ingress-sys-prom -o yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  annotations:
    kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration: |
      {"apiVersion":"networking.k8s.io/v1","kind":"NetworkPolicy","metadata":{"annotations":{},"name":"private-ingress-sys-prom","namespace":"partner-registration"},"spec":{"ingress":[{"from":[{"namespaceSelector":{"matchLabels":{"name":"sys-prom"}}}],"ports":[{"port":"metrics"}]}],"podSelector":{},"policyTypes":["Ingress"]}}
  creationTimestamp: "2021-03-26T10:52:05Z"
  generation: 3
  name: private-ingress-sys-prom
  namespace: partner-registration
  resourceVersion: "3454111968"
  uid: 26a53b37-53e3-4a8d-92dd-8e17836b087d

        matchLabels:
          name: sys-prom
    ports:
    - port: metrics
      protocol: TCP
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
```

Testing the connection from Prometheus I observe the following results for member 0 and 1:

```console
$ kubectl --context prod-aws -n sys-prom exec -ti prometheus-system-0 -c prometheus -- wget -T2 -O - http://10.2.142.58:8099/__/metrics | head -4
Connecting to 10.2.142.58:8099 (10.2.142.58:8099)
writing to stdout

Connecting to 10.2.13.56:8099 (10.2.13.56:8099)
writing to stdout
# HELP go_gc_duration_seconds A summary of the pause duration of garbage collection cycles.
# TYPE go_gc_duration_seconds summary
```

And a timeout for member 2 (running initContainer sidecar):

```console
$ kubectl --context prod-aws -n sys-prom exec -ti prometheus-system-0 -c prometheus -- wget -T2 -O - http://10.2.2.53:8099/__/metrics | head -4
Connecting to 10.2.2.53:8099 (10.2.2.53:8099)
wget: download timed out
command terminated with exit code 1
```

If I apply the following patch:

```patch
diff --git a/prod-aws/partner-registration/02-network-policies.yaml b/prod-aws/partner-registration/02-network-policies.yaml
index 9d3ea45d86..c685cc8667 100644
--- a/prod-aws/partner-registration/02-network-policies.yaml
+++ b/prod-aws/partner-registration/02-network-policies.yaml
@@ -43,7 +43,7 @@ spec:
             matchLabels:
               name: sys-prom
       ports:
-        - port: metrics
+        - port: 8099
 ---

 ---
```

Then I'm able to establish a connection with cockroachdb-2:

```console

Connecting to 10.2.2.53:8099 (10.2.2.53:8099)
writing to stdout
# HELP go_gc_duration_seconds A summary of the pause duration of garbage collection cycles.
```

### What did you expect to happen?

named port in the initContainer spec allows the traffic if it matches config of the NetworkPolicy.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Hi. I've researched this problem and here's how it works:
1) The nfs Plugin mounts nfs-share in volumes/kubernetes.io~nfs/\<pv-name>
2) subpather mounts volumes/kubernetes.io~nfs/\<pv-name>/\<subpath> to volume-subpaths/\<pv-name>/\<ctr-name>/\<mount-index>

In fact, subpather runs the mount -o bind command...
That's how it looks in the code:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1608dc2b0928fc69a9923716a305612746dbec55/pkg/volume/util/subpath/subpath_linux.go#L228-L233

When using the --bind option to mount one directory to another, the original mounting options are not automatically transferred to the new mounting point. 
That is, when using mount --bind, the mount options, including the NFS-specific nosuid, will not be saved automatically on the new mount.
However, these options continue to work "in the background", as they are active for the original mounting point.
So it turns out that there is a problem only with displaying all the options, of course if we consider this a problem? 
It seems to me that this can be easily fixed by simply reading the parameters from the first mount and adding them to the second.
I can do a pr
/assign

In my cluster (created by `hack/local-up-cluster.sh`), I can see both the main mount + subpath mount retain `nosuid` in their /proc/mounts entries:

```
192.168.122.1:/home/jsafrane/tmp on /var/lib/kubelet/pods/559a34f5-226a-48ae-8dbe-a93458404b68/volumes/kubernetes.io~nfs/nfs-pv type nfs4 (rw,nosuid,relatime,vers=4.2,rsize=1048576,wsize=1048576,namlen=255,hard,proto=tcp,timeo=600,retrans=2,sec=sys,clientaddr=192.168.122.75,local_lock=none,addr=192.168.122.1)
192.168.122.1:/home/jsafrane/tmp/subdir on /var/lib/kubelet/pods/559a34f5-226a-48ae-8dbe-a93458404b68/volume-subpaths/nfs-pv/busybox/0 type nfs4 (rw,nosuid,relatime,vers=4.2,rsize=1048576,wsize=1048576,namlen=255,hard,proto=tcp,timeo=600,retrans=2,sec=sys,clientaddr=192.168.122.75,local_lock=none,addr=192.168.122.1)
```

Kubernetes 1.31 beta (but I don't think it matters), Fedora 39, Kernel 6.8.10-200.fc39.x86_64
It could be caused either by the kernel or KIND.

`mount` man page says:

> Note that the filesystem mount options maintained by the kernel will remain the same as those on the original mount point. The userspace mount options (e.g., _netdev) will not be copied by mount and it’s necessary to explicitly specify the options on the mount command line.
...
> It’s also possible to change nosuid, nodev, noexec, noatime, nodiratime, relatime and nosymfollow VFS entry flags via ...


I interpret it as `nosuid` should be copied by default, but can be explicitly changed in a bind mount.

2. Working cluster on bare metal

I think so. In the near future, I will be able to check this and make a new PR or change the old one.

title: Static pods with restartPolicy: OnFailure remain pending if kubelet restarts after container create but before start.
body:
### What happened?

Given a static pod with `restartPolicy: OnFailure`, and  a Kubelet crash while re-creating a failed container in the static pod, the pod may remain pending indefinitely.

1. Run a cluster with the patch at https://github.com/hoskeri/kubernetes/commit/60b103a1df145a688a72ebe1473deddec57109e0. The patch causes kubelet to crash when attempting to start a container that's been created after a failure.
2. Start a static pod with `restartPolicy: OnFailure`.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: staticpod-failure-tester
spec: 
  restartPolicy: OnFailure
  hostNetwork: true
  initContainers:
  - name: staticpod-failure-init-1
    image: "debian:unstable"
    command:
    - echo 
    - "staticpod-failure-tester-init"
  containers:
  - name: staticpod-failure-tester-main
    image: "redis:latest"
    command:
    - "redis-server"
```


4. Arm the crash to occur on the next StartContainer of our container.

echo -n staticpod-failure-tester-main > /run/crash-container-names

6. Kill the shim process and `crictl stopp $pod`. 

(Careful, modify the command to be more specific if other containers are running in your env)

`kill -9 $SHIM_PID; crictl pods -q|xargs crictl stopp`

7. Kubelet should create a replacement container for the killed container in the same sandbox.

9. Kubelet crashes and restarts on StartContainer.

10. After the first crash, kubelet will not trigger the crash again, because it will not attempt a StartContainer again. 
Instead, `computePodActions` wants to stop the existing sandbox, but this does not converge because containerd ignores the `StopContainer` request. 

```
info msg="Container to stop \"469b9ca1059f90783892692b7ecf22b967d015a390446b44ee29894026b7e46a\" must be in running or unknown state, current state \"CONTAINER_CREATED\""
```

```
kuberuntime_manager.go:1058] "computePodActions got for pod" podActions="KillPod: true, CreateSandbox: false, UpdatePodResources: false, Attempt: 3, InitContainersToStart: [], ContainersToStart: [], EphemeralContainersToStart: [],ContainersToUpdate: map[], ContainersToKill: map[]" pod="default/staticpod-failure-tester-i-ea7ab8cd-6939-4748-b544-21d797194f5e"
```

11. The pod remains `Pending` indefinitely.

The real-world version of the above sequence involves a reboot of control plane host vm while Kubelet is still recovering pods from a previous crash - so two reboots in quick succession. 

Based on my reading of the code, it seems to me that the core issue is in the `containerSucceeded` function treats an uninitialized container as having succeeded. We incorrectly read the golang zero value of `containerStatus.ExitCode` as a successful exit code of `0` from the container. 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8f80e0146726c42edefdfaeda6123872a5ec0981/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L535

This is not an issue if the restartPolicy is `Always` because https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8f80e0146726c42edefdfaeda6123872a5ec0981/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L851 is not reached in that case.



### What did you expect to happen?

The static pod should either end at a terminal phase, or restart the successfully.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

See reproduction steps in the main report. 

Here's a strawman change that fixes the issue for my test case.

@hoskeri it seems like there are two issues:
 1. kubelet tries to kill the container because it thinks that the container is in a running state. Did you see containerd/cri reporting the container as running? If so, there might be a containerd issue.
 2. kubelet not starting the a new replacement container because it considered the pod succeeded.

I agree, we are switching the restartPolicy to Always as the fix for this issue in our application. The earlier setting may have been an oversight, or a misunderstanding of what OnFailure does. 

However, I think this is still a bug, or atleast a footgun that needs to be documented. 

- restartPolicy: OnFailure is definitely applicable to jobs/cronjobs, for example.

No, it did not, the container was not started after create, and the state as seen by kubelet remained at 'created'. 

> 2. kubelet not starting the a new replacement container because it considered the pod succeeded.
> 
> Did you verify that with restart policy "always", the problem wouldn't occur (meaning (1) wouldn't block (2))?

I have not verified this, but I think restartPolicy: Always works because the 'created' container is started, and then killPod can succeed in killing the now running container. 
 
> > Out of curiosity, what is the use case for running a static pod with a restart policy other than Always? It seems like anything other than always would be somewhat arbitrary, since the state would be tracked unreliably?
> 
> +1 to this question too.

We are switching to Always for our application, but there might be other cases (see my other comment) where this might still be a problem.

> No, it did not, the container was not started after create, and the state as seen by kubelet remained at 'created'.

In this case, kubelet shouldn't even try to stop the container. I was confused as why kubelet repeatedly trying to do that (not just a race condition during a specific window).

> I have not verified this, but I think restartPolicy: Always works because the 'created' container is started, and then killPod can succeed in killing the now running container.

It sounds like there are some legit issues here that should be fixed, but I wonder if we should also stop supporting non-`Always` restart policies on static pods. I think all static pods should be restart: Always, so I'm not sure this is a case we currently want to support. We even are in the process of removing the `runOnce` kubelet mode, which allows them to be run to completion. What use case for onFailure do you have?
/cc

> I think all static pods should be restart: Always, so I'm not sure this is a case we currently want to support. We even are in the process of removing the `runOnce` kubelet mode, which allows them to be run to completion. What use case for onFailure do you have?

I don't have a use-case for OnFailure really, and I have switched the workload where I discovered this issue to be `Always`. 

But: While I investigated this in the context of static pods, I have a suspicion this applies to api hosted restart-on-failure containers as well. I'll see if I can reproduce this in a non-static pod. 

Here's the core issue I think: How does kubelet determine a container has "run to completion"? 

Based on the code, I think the intention is to get the container status from CRI, and check that the container has exited with a status code `0`. 

The bug is that we only check that the exit code is 0, but do not also verify that the container has exited. If the container has any state other than 'Running', we incorrectly read the golang zero value from the ExitCode field. 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a2106b5f73fe9352f7bc0520788855d57fc301e1/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L540

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/126420 oughta fix this.

nodes.title: kuberuntime_manager: fix container success check.
nodes.body:
When evaluating whether a container ran to completion, we only check whether the CRI container status `ExitCode` is 0.

But, the ExitCode is only meaningful if the container has actually run and exited.

There are other states, eg: `Created` where the container runtime never set an ExitCode - we shouldn't read it in that case.

/kind bug

Fixes #123839

```release-note
NONE
```

title: Kubelet - failed to initialize top level QOS containers: root container [kubepods] doesn't exist
body:
### What happened?

Starting the kubelet the first time after a system reboot,  the kubelet fails with:
`E0125 00:20:56.003890    2172 kubelet.go:1466] "Failed to start ContainerManager" err="failed to initialize top level QOS containers: root container [kubepods] doesn't exist"`

Which, sort of is a lie.   The root cause is actually that `cpuset` does not exist in `/sys/fs/cgroup/cgroup.subtree_control` 

After the kubelet exits, systemd restarts in,  and then all is fine after that,  until the next time the OS is restarted.  

I tried to track it down,  create.go does add the cpuset to `cgroup.subtree_control`,  and it remains there until `common.go:setUnitProperties()` is executed,  at which time `cpuset` appears to be disabled and disappears.  The other controllers are unaffected.   On the subsequent kubelet restart, `cpuset` does get added again,  and remains after the call to setUnitProperties().   

### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect the kubelet to start and not exit on all starts of the kubelet. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

The OS I am using is RHEL 9 on s390x.   
1) Boot the OS
2) Start the kubelet (I start with `kubeadm init` or `kubeadm join`.
3) Observer the kubelet starts,  fails, and then restarts.   Subsequent restarts of the kubelet are successful until the OS rebooted. (Likely due to after a reboot, the /sys/fs/cgroups is fresh,  unlike subsequent restarts of the kubelet)


### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

basically: we've figured out that this issue happens because libcontainer doesn't initialize the cpuset cgroup for the kubepods slice when the kubelet initially calls into it to do so. It's possible this is a limitation in the dbus API: how do you ask systemd to create a cgroup that is effectively empty?

if we delegate: we are telling systemd to leave our cgroups alone, and not remove the "unneeded" cpuset cgroup.

Haven't seen this error for a long time, I can close it if no new ideas here.

I think the issue is obsolete with https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/123935, as we no longer should expose errors from direct etcd watch.

Background:
Error `Internal error occurred: etcd event received with PrevKv=nil` comes from fact that etcd doesn't guarantee that it will always provide PrevKV, while K8s requires it. When we allowed K8s clients to open watch directly to etcd in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/115096 those errors were exposed to client. However this was deemed unsafe for many reasons (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/123448, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/123072). Now the errors will be handled by K8s watch cache and not exposed to clients.

title: readiness probe is not scheduled as configured periodSeconds
body:
### What happened? **Below pod yaml file was deployed. From probe logs we see probe is getting scheduled more than once in 30 sec duration of perodSeconds configured for readinessProbe. At times it gets scheduled twice within 5 seconds though 30 sec is configured as periodSeconds** apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: labels: test: readiness name: ready1 spec: containers: - name: readiness image: busybox command: ["top"] readinessProbe: exec: command: - /tmp/probe.sh initialDelaySeconds: 3 failureThreshold: 1 successThreshold: 1 periodSeconds: 30 **/tmp/probe.sh was added as executable after doing exec to pod to simulate the issue.** / # cat /tmp/probe.sh #!/bin/sh echo "Probe at `date`" >> /tmp/probe.log exit 1 / # tail -f /tmp/probe.log Probe at Fri Jun 16 07:16:16 UTC 2023 Probe at Fri Jun 16 07:16:35 UTC 2023 Probe at Fri Jun 16 07:17:05 UTC 2023 Probe at Fri Jun 16 07:17:19 UTC 2023 Probe at Fri Jun 16 07:17:35 UTC 2023 ### What did you expect to happen? Expect readinessProbe to be scheduled acurately as periodSeconds. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? Hi @mochizuki875 
I think you used ">" instead of append ">>" in /mnt/probe.sh. You can see in below logs it got scheduled twice in 5 min 12:48:21 & 12:48:26.

Log in my environment:
<log>

exit 1

It seems to be intentional from reading the code.
`ReadinessProbe` will be executed by two triggers 

- Constant interval(depends on `periodSeconds` which is `ReadinessProbe`'s field)
  - `probeTicker.C` channel will receive value when `periodSeconds` has passed by `time.Ticker`.
- `Pod` sync occur
  - `w.manualTriggerCh` channel will receive value when `UpdatePod()` is called with `Pod` sync and `ReadinessProbe has not be success`.  (as @SataQiu said)

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0a82bdbfdb1b8dd644d242b39a257d14fa5bf6b0/pkg/kubelet/prober/worker.go#L179-L189

rf:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/96731
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/98376
